entry: Gender identity differing from the sex assigned at birth. Transgender has no universally accepted definition and can serve as an umbrella term for binary trans men and trans women, and sometimes for [[Non-binary|non-binary]] people. It is distinct from [[Sexual orientation]]. Generally, less than 1% of the world's population is transgender, with figures ranging from <0.1% to 0.6%, though estimates vary widely. Many transgender people experience gender dysphoria and seek hormone replacement therapy, gender-affirming surgery, or [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]], though not all desire or can access these. Legal status varies by jurisdiction, and in many places transgender people are not legally protected from discrimination. Medical approaches are debated: the American Medical Association and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming care, including for some minors, while reviews in the United Kingdom, Sweden, Finland, and Norway rate the evidence for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones in adolescents as low quality and restrict routine use.

Intellectual and cultural movement advocating technological enhancement of human capacities. Transhumanism advocates using existing, emerging, and speculative technologies to extend longevity and improve cognition, health, and well-being. Key areas of inquiry include [[Nanotechnology|nanotechnology]], [[Biotechnology|biotechnology]], and [[Information technology|information technology]]. Some transhumanists envision humans becoming "posthumans," and others focus on reducing existential risks, including those posed by artificial superintelligence and pandemics. Biologist Julian Huxley popularized the term in a 1957 essay. Max More formulated transhumanism as a class of philosophies beginning in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Critics argue that it revives eugenic ideology under the banner of technological progress and individual choice.

[[Semiconductor device]] used to amplify or switch electrical signals and power. A voltage or current applied to one pair of terminals controls current through another pair, and transistors are the key active components of modern [[Electronics|electronics]]. The first working device, a point-contact transistor, was invented in 1947 by [[John Bardeen]], Walter Brattain, and [[William Shockley]] at [[Bell Labs]], who shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. The most widely used type, the metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor ([[MOSFET]]), was invented at Bell Labs between 1955 and 1960. Compared with the [[Vacuum tube|vacuum tube]], transistors are generally smaller and require less power, paving the way for smaller, cheaper radios, calculators, and [[Computer|computers]].

Series of chemical elements in the d-block of the [[Periodic table|periodic table]], groups 3 to 12. Transition metals are lustrous, with good electrical and thermal conductivity. Most, except those in groups 11 and 12, are hard, strong, and have high melting and boiling temperatures. They form compounds in two or more oxidation states and many colored coordination complexes, and many are used as [[Catalysis|catalysts]] and in [[Alloy|alloys]]. Most are strongly paramagnetic. Elements ferromagnetic near room temperature are [[Iron]], [[Nickel]], and cobalt (transition metals) and [[Gadolinium]] (an inner transition metal). The [[Lanthanide]] and [[Actinide]] elements are called inner transition metals. English chemist Charles Rugeley Bury first used the word "transition" in this context in 1921.

Communication of the meaning of a source-language text by means of an equivalent target-language text. English distinguishes translating written texts from interpreting oral or signed communication. Translators always risk carrying source-language words, grammar, or syntax into the target language, though such spill-overs have sometimes enriched languages with calques and loanwords. [[Cicero]] and [[Horace]] cautioned against word-for-word translation in 1st-century BCE [[Rome]]. [[Ancient Greek|Ancient Greeks]] distinguished metaphrase (literal translation) from paraphrase, and [[John Dryden]] later described translation as a judicious blend of the two. Since the 1940s, efforts to automate translation have achieved varying success, and the [[Internet]] has fostered a worldwide market for translation services.

Cellular process of protein synthesis. [[Ribosome|Ribosomes]] decode messenger [[RNA]] (mRNA) to build a polypeptide chain, adding one [[Amino acid|amino acid]] for each three-nucleotide codon according to the [[Genetic code]]. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry the amino acids to the ribosome, where each tRNA's anticodon pairs with a complementary mRNA codon. Aminoacyl tRNA synthetases attach the correct amino acid to each tRNA. The chain then folds into an active [[Protein]]. Translation has three stages: initiation, elongation, and termination. Ribosomes are multisubunit structures of ribosomal RNA and proteins. In [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], the small (40S) and large (60S) ribosomal subunits join before translation begins. The entire process is called [[Gene expression|gene expression]].

Representation of text from one [[Writing system|writing system]] in the script of another. Transliteration conveys how a word is pronounced so that readers can approximate its sounds, and it does not change pronunciation. For example, the Greek term Ελληνική Δημοκρατία is transliterated into the [[Latin script]] as Hellēnikḗ Dēmokratía. It differs from [[Translation|translation]], which conveys meaning, and from transcription, which phonetically approximates sound using the [[International Phonetic Alphabet]]. Most systematic transliterations are one-to-one, so the original spelling can be reconstructed, but unsystematic transliteration is common, as for Burmese. Standard systems exist for many script pairs, though conventions and author preferences vary. Angle brackets, ⟨ ⟩, set off transliterations.

One of the main protocols of the [[Internet protocol suite]], providing reliable, ordered, and error-checked delivery of a stream of [[Byte|bytes]] between applications on hosts communicating over an [[Internet Protocol|IP]] network. Major applications such as the [[World Wide Web]], email, file transfer, and [[Streaming media|streaming media]] rely on it. TCP is connection-oriented: a three-way handshake establishes a connection, and retransmission and [[Error detection and correction|error detection]] add reliability at the cost of latency. Applications that do not need reliable delivery may use the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) instead. TCP also employs network congestion avoidance, but it has known vulnerabilities, including denial-of-service attacks, connection hijacking, and reset attacks.

Landlocked, unrecognized breakaway state in Eastern Europe, officially the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic. Internationally recognized as part of [[Moldova]], it controls a narrow strip between the Dniester River and the Moldova–Ukraine border, with Tiraspol as its capital and largest city. The Pridnestrovian Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic was established in 1990, in hopes that it would remain within the [[Soviet Union]] if Moldova sought unification with Romania. A military conflict with Moldova began in March 1992 and ended in a July ceasefire. Transnistria is a de facto independent semi-presidential republic with its own government, parliament, military, police, currency, and vehicle registration. It is one of three post-Soviet "frozen conflict" zones, along with [[Abkhazia]] and [[South Ossetia]]. In March 2022, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe adopted a resolution defining the territory as under military occupation by [[Russia]].

Physical property of allowing light to pass through a material. Transparency allows light to pass without appreciable [[Scattering|scattering]], so on a macroscopic scale its photons follow [[Snell's law]]. Translucency allows light through with or without scattering, because a translucent material is made up of components with different [[Refractive index|indices of refraction]]. The opposite of translucency is opacity. Materials that do not transmit light are opaque, and many absorb certain frequencies of the [[Visible spectrum|visible spectrum]] while reflecting others, which produces color. [[Glass|Plate glass]] and clean water are transparent. Transparency can provide almost perfect [[Camouflage|camouflage]]; many marine animals, such as [[Jellyfish]], are highly transparent.

Movement of water through a [[Plant|plant]] and its [[Evaporation|evaporation]] from aerial parts such as leaves, stems, and flowers. Transpiration is passive and requires no energy expense by the plant. It cools the plant, changes osmotic pressure of cells, and enables mass flow of mineral nutrients. Of the water taken up by the roots, 97–99.5% is lost through transpiration and guttation. As water evaporates from the leaf surface, it pulls on adjacent water molecules, creating a continuous flow through the xylem. When water uptake is less than water loss, plants close small pores called [[Stoma|stomata]], which slows nutrient uptake and CO₂ absorption, limiting [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] and growth.

Medical procedure in which an organ, tissue, or cells are moved from one organism to a recipient, often to replace a damaged or missing function. Transplants between subjects of the same [[Species|species]] are allografts, from living or cadaveric donors. [[Kidney|Kidneys]] are the most commonly transplanted organs worldwide, followed by [[Liver|liver]] and [[Heart|heart]]. Corneas and musculoskeletal grafts are the most common tissue transplants, outnumbering organ transplants more than tenfold. Donors may be living or deceased from [[Brain death|brain death]] or circulatory death. Transplant rejection, an immune response to the new organ, can cause failure; it is reduced by matching donor and recipient and by immunosuppressant drugs. Only 10–20% of worldwide needs are met. The [[United States]] reached one million cumulative transplants on September 9, 2022, according to the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network.

Cryptographic protocol providing secure communications over a [[Computer network|computer network]], such as the [[Internet]]. It is widely used for [[Email|email]], instant messaging, and voice over IP, but its use in securing [[HTTPS]] is the most visible. TLS aims to provide privacy, integrity, and authenticity through cryptography, including certificates, between communicating applications. A handshake lets client and server agree on cipher settings and a session-specific shared key with which further communication is [[Encryption|encrypted]]. TLS was first defined in 1999; the current version is TLS 1.3, defined in August 2018. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) applies it to datagram-based applications.

Historical region in [[Central Europe]], encompassing central [[Romania]]. Its natural eastern and southern border is the Carpathian Mountains, and it is known for its Carpathian scenery, medieval towns, and multicultural character. King [[Stephen I of Hungary|Stephen I]] asserted claims over Hungarian lands, and Transylvania became part of the Kingdom of Hungary in 1002. The Principality of Transylvania emerged in 1570 and was largely a vassal state of the [[Ottoman Empire]] during most of the 16th and 17th centuries. The [[Habsburg monarchy]] gained it in 1690. After [[World War I]], a national assembly proclaimed union with Romania on 1 December 1918, and the region became part of Romania under the Treaty of Trianon in 1920. In popular culture, Transylvania is associated with [[Vampire|vampires]] through [[Bram Stoker]]'s 1897 novel *Dracula*.

Usually convex [[Quadrilateral|quadrilateral]] with at least one pair of parallel sides, called bases; the other two sides are legs. Under the inclusive definition used by most mathematicians, every parallelogram, including [[Rhombus]] and [[Square]], is a trapezoid. Many school texts use an exclusive definition requiring exactly one pair of parallel sides. The name derives from the Greek word for "table." In [[Euclid's Elements]] (c. 300 BC), a trapezium was any quadrilateral not already classed as a square, oblong, rhombus, or rhomboid. In British English it is called a trapezium. Its area is half the sum of the bases times the height.

Movement of people between distant geographical locations. Travel may be by foot, [[Car|automobile]], [[Train|train]], boat, bus, [[Airplane|airplane]], or ship, with or without luggage, one way or round trip. Motives include recreation, [[Pilgrimage|pilgrimages]], business, trade, health care, and migration. Wealthy Greeks and Romans traveled for leisure to summer homes in cities such as [[Pompeii]]. Travel in the Middle Ages was hard but important to the economy, and pilgrimages were common in both the European and Islamic worlds. The 1492 voyage of [[Christopher Columbus|Columbus]] from Spain to the New World took over 10 weeks, while aircraft later allowed travel from Spain to the United States overnight.

NP-hard problem in combinatorial optimization. Given cities and the distances between each pair, the travelling salesman problem asks for the shortest route that visits each city exactly once and returns to the origin city. It is one of the most intensively studied problems in optimization and a benchmark for [[Heuristic|heuristics]] and exact algorithms, which can solve instances with tens of thousands of cities; instances with millions of cities can be approximated within a small fraction of 1%. Applications include [[Logistics|logistics]], microchip manufacturing, and DNA sequencing. In [[Astronomy|astronomy]], telescopes observing many sources must minimize the time spent moving between them.

Adventure novel by Scottish novelist [[Robert Louis Stevenson]], published in 1883. Set in the 18th century, it follows Jim Hawkins, the innkeeper's son near [[Bristol]], who finds a map to pirate Captain Flint's buried treasure. Jim sails on the *Hispaniola*, where the one-legged cook Long John Silver leads a planned mutiny. It was first serialized in *Young Folks* from 1881 to 1882 as *Treasure Island, or the Mutiny of the Hispaniola*. It is one of the most frequently dramatized and adapted novels and shaped pirate imagery, including deserted tropical islands, treasure maps marked with an "X," and one-legged seamen with [[Parrot|parrots]] on their shoulders.

International agreement between [[Sovereign state|sovereign states]] or other subjects of [[International law|international law]]. Only legally binding documents count as treaties, though they may be called protocols, covenants, conventions, or pacts. Treaties may be bilateral or multilateral and bind only the parties that sign and ratify them. A treaty may be invalid if it violates a peremptory norm (*jus cogens*), such as permitting a war of aggression. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT), adopted on 22 May 1969 and in force from 27 January 1980, codifies rules for making, interpreting, amending, and ending treaties. Under the UN Charter, treaties must be registered with the United Nations to be invoked before the [[International Court of Justice]]. A bilateral treaty can have many parties: each of the bilateral treaties between [[Switzerland]] and the [[European Union]] has seventeen.

Agreement ending the [[American Revolutionary War]], signed in [[Paris]] on September 3, 1783. Representatives of King [[George III]] and of the [[United States]] signed it, recognizing the [[Thirteen Colonies]] as free, sovereign, and independent states. Only its Article 1 remains in force. The treaty set boundaries between British North America, later [[Canada]], and the United States on lines the British called "exceedingly generous." It also covered fishing rights and the restoration of property and prisoners of war. American negotiators included [[Benjamin Franklin]], [[John Adams]], John Jay, and Henry Laurens.

Treaty of 1494 dividing newly discovered lands outside Europe between Portugal and Castile. Signed in Tordesillas, Spain, on June 7, 1494, it set a meridian 370 leagues (c. 2,100 km or 1,300 mi) west of the [[Cape Verde]] islands. Lands to the east belonged to Portugal and lands to the west to Castile. The line lay about halfway between Cape Verde and the islands [[Christopher Columbus]] had visited, which he thought were Cipangu and Antillia but were in fact [[Cuba]] and [[Hispaniola]]. It modified an earlier bull by [[Pope Alexander VI]]. Portugal and Spain largely respected it, but Indigenous peoples of the Americas did not acknowledge it. Pope Julius II ratified it in 1506, and [[UNESCO]] added it to its Memory of the World register in 2007.

Peace treaty signed on 28 June 1919 in the [[Palace of Versailles]] that ended the state of war between Germany and most Allied Powers in [[World War I]]. It required Germany to disarm, make territorial concessions, and pay reparations to the Entente powers. Article 231, the "War Guilt" clause, has Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage of the war. [[John Maynard Keynes]] called the treaty too harsh, while French Marshal [[Ferdinand Foch]] criticized it for treating Germany too leniently. The United States never ratified it. The Dawes and Young Plans later reduced reparations. Bitter German resentment of the treaty helped the rise of the [[Nazi Party]] and eventually [[World War II]].

Siege engine, a type of [[Catapult]] with a hinged arm and a [[Sling (weapon)|sling]] for launching projectiles. The traction trebuchet, or mangonel, used manpower to swing its arm and appeared in China by the 4th century BC. The later counterweight trebuchet appeared in Christian and Muslim lands around the Mediterranean in the 12th century and was carried back to China by the [[Mongols]] in the 13th century. Its design launched projectiles of greater weight or range than a traditional catapult, making it a common siege engine until [[Gunpowder]] arrived. King [[Edward I]]'s massive trebuchet, Warwolf, was deployed in 1304 to shatter defenses at Stirling Castle.

Land warfare fought from occupied lines of trenches that shelter combatants from enemy fire and artillery. Although used in antiquity, it fully developed in the 17th century. During the American Civil War (1861–1865), sieges at Vicksburg and Petersburg showed soldiers digging in to avoid shelling. The tactic reached its most extreme form in World War I, when [[Machine gun|machine guns]], rapid-fire [[Artillery|artillery]], and barbed wire froze the front lines on the [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]] into a kilometer-long system of trenches. The first day of the [[Battle of the Somme]] in 1916 produced over 57,000 British casualties. Tanks eventually broke the deadlock in 1918.

South African comedian, writer, producer, and [[Television|television]] host. Born in [[Johannesburg]], Noah began his career in [[South Africa]] in 2008. He hosted *The Daily Show* on Comedy Central from 2015 to 2022, succeeding [[Jon Stewart]]. His [[Autobiography|autobiography]] *Born a Crime* was published in 2016. He has won various awards, including two Primetime Emmy Awards, and has hosted the [[Grammy Awards]]. In 2018, *Time* magazine named him one of the 100 most influential people in the world.
